newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Imperial scoffs at dawn raid talk. [CORRECTED 13:06 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Imperial scoffs at dawn raid talk. [CORRECTED 13:06 GMT]

text.p: Imperial Tobacco Plc, spun off from its former parent group Hanson Plc two days ago, dismissed speculation of a dawn raid on its shares which have surged and attracted massive trading volumes since demerging.

Robert Dyrbus, finance director at Imperial, said in an interview on Thursday that the share price rally in the last three sessions has been due to strong interest from U.S. investors where 30 percent of the stock is held.
Commenting on the dawn raid rumours, he said: "We've seen nothing unusual in the share activity."
Imperial had been expected to open trading on Tuesday at between 370 and 380 pence per share, but instead opened at 390 and ended its first session ahead at 393 pence.
By 1119 GMT on Thursday, Imperial had risen to 426, up 22 pence, with trading volumes at 6.8 million shares.
(Corrects from 60.8 million).

One trader said "Imperial was always een as a possible bid target, it was the plum bit of Hanson. we thought 390p was a fair opening price but anything over 400p starts to included a bid premium." He added "any bidder would probably have to pay between 500p and 520p."
But Dyrbus said there had been no evidence of bid interest.
But the finance chief attributed the share price surge to strong demand in the U.S. after a recent series of investor roadshows by the Hanson team which visited about seven U.S. cities in five days.
"We're just seeing a lot of demand on both sides of the Atlantic. When we started the demerger process we assumed that in the U.S. we would see a sell-off," said Dyrbus.
"But instead investors see us as having all the characteristics of a tobacco stock -- strong cash flow, capital expenditure -- and no exposure to U.S. litigation," he said.
Dyrbus added the biggest recorded investor remained PDFM.
On the subject of the group court action being brought against Imperial in the UK courts by cancer sufferers, the finance chief said "we and our legal advisers have confidence in our defence."

Commenting on the company's strategy now that it has split off from the once-mighty hanson conglomerate group, Dyrbus said Ipmerial had told investors at its roadshows that export-led growth was the key.
"Gareth Davis (chief executive) stated he would be disappointed if 25 percent of our activities didn't come from foreign operations by the end of the decade," said Dyrbus.
Last year, 13 percent of earnings and 15 percent of volumes came from overseas business.
Ipmerial's concentration of business in the UK market has been interpreted as a weakness by some analysts. The UK is seen as a fairly mature market, with little growth potential.
The company's bigger rivals have already secured footholds in important emerging markets like China, India and Asia-Pacific countries making it difficult for Imperial to make inroads.
But Dyrbus denied the company was on the backfoot in these regions. "We are a late entrant to international markets -- that's certainly true. But we are growing that business.
"These markets are so large that even a small niche prescence could have substantial impact on us."
